final_text: AWS Application Load Balancers close a connection that has been idle (no data in either direction) for the idle timeout, 60 seconds by default and configurable from 1 to 4000 seconds. For long operations, AWS advises sending at least 1 byte before each idle period ends and setting the application's own idle timeout above the load balancer's.
note: Opened ALB attributes page: 'send at least 1 byte of data before each idle timeout period elapses'; 'configure the idle timeout of your application to be larger than the idle timeout configured for the load balancer'; default 60 s; 'The valid range is 1 through 4000 seconds.' All figures match.

final_text: TCP keep-alives are optional in the TCP standard; if implemented they must be off by default, and the interval must default to no less than two hours (RFC 9293). So unless the application sends data or its own heartbeats, an idle TCP connection may not notice for hours that the peer is gone.
note: Opened RFC 9293 3.8.4: keep-alives 'MAY' be included (MAY-5), 'MUST default to off (MUST-25)', interval 'MUST default to no less than two hours (MUST-28)'. First sentence confirmed. The second sentence ('TCP itself has no built-in liveness detection, so applications usually add their own heartbeats') is not in the RFC; softened to what follows from the cited text.

final_text: HTTP/1.1 uses persistent connections by default: several requests and responses share one connection until someone sends 'Connection: close'. Under HTTP/1.0 the connection stayed open only if the 'keep-alive' option was sent and honored (RFC 9112, section 9.3).
note: Opened RFC 9112 9.3: 'HTTP/1.1 defaults to the use of "persistent connections"'; the 'close' option ends persistence; for HTTP/1.0 the connection persists only if the 'keep-alive' option is present and the recipient wishes to honor it. Matches; useful because the item says HTTP terminates after the response.

final_text: gRPC sends HTTP/2 PING frames as keepalives so a long-lived connection is not treated as idle by proxies or load balancers. On the server, MAX_CONNECTION_IDLE and MAX_CONNECTION_AGE (both infinite by default) can close connections deliberately. Note that AWS Application Load Balancers do not count HTTP/2 PINGs as activity for their idle timeout.
note: Opened grpc.io keepalive guide: PING frames 'periodically sending a PING frame'; long-lived connections 'might be considered as idle by proxy or load balancers'; MAX_CONNECTION_IDLE and MAX_CONNECTION_AGE default 'INT_MAX (Infinite)'. Opened ALB attributes page: 'Application Load Balancers do not support HTTP/2 PING frames. These do not reset the connection idle timeout.' All claims supported.

final_text: Go's standard net/http server cancels a request's Context when the client's connection closes, when the request is canceled over HTTP/2, or when the handler returns. A handler that passes this context to its database or downstream calls stops work when the user goes away.
note: Opened pkg.go.dev net/http (read past offset 100000): Request.Context doc says 'For incoming server requests, the context is canceled when the client's connection closes,' the request is canceled (HTTP/2), or ServeHTTP returns. Matches.

final_text: Canceling a BigQuery job is not guaranteed: the job may already have finished or be in a stage that cannot be canceled, and you can still be charged depending on when it was canceled. Cancellation usually completes in under a minute.
note: Opened BigQuery managing-jobs: 'Even if the job can be canceled, success is not guaranteed.'; 'You can still incur costs after canceling a job depending on the stage at which it was canceled.'; 'It usually takes less than a minute to complete a job cancellation.' Matches.

final_text: Nginx's default upstream method is weighted round robin: each server has 'weight' (default 1), so a server with weight=5 next to two weight-1 servers gets 5 of every 7 requests.
note: Opened nginx upstream module: 'By default, requests are distributed between the servers using a weighted round-robin balancing method'; example 'each 7 requests ... 5 requests go to backend1'; weight 'by default, 1'. Matches.

final_text: An RDS Multi-AZ DB instance keeps a synchronous standby in another Availability Zone for automatic failover, but AWS notes this 'isn't a scaling solution': the standby cannot serve reads. Redundancy (no single point of failure) and scale-out (more capacity) are separate properties.
note: Opened RDS Multi-AZ page: 'automatically provisions and maintains a synchronous standby replica in a different Availability Zone'; note: 'The high availability option isn't a scaling solution for read-only scenarios. You can't use a standby replica to serve read traffic.' Quote 'isn't a scaling solution' is verbatim. Good counter-example for L-0038.

final_text: Google's SRE book warns that queries per second is a poor capacity unit because the cost of different queries varies and changes as the software changes. It recommends measuring capacity directly in resources; CPU consumption alone works well as the provisioning signal in most cases.
note: Opened SRE book 'Handling Overload': QPS/static features 'often makes for a poor metric'; 'A better solution is to measure capacity directly in available resources'; 'simply using CPU consumption as the signal for provisioning works well' in most cases. Matches; useful nuance but tangential to the item.

final_text: Redis 8.4 added 'DELEX key IFEQ value', which deletes a lock key only if it still holds the caller's random value. This replaces the Lua compare-and-delete script that earlier versions needed.
note: Opened Redis distributed-locks page: 'DELEX key IFEQ my_random_value' and 'The DELEX command was introduced in Redis 8.4. On previous Redis versions, this could be accomplished with the following Lua script'. Accurate, but it duplicates A-LDA-03, which is attached to the item that actually teaches the Lua compare-and-delete (L-0273); L-0272 is a generic remark about edge cases.

final_text: Majority quorums are what buy fault tolerance: a Raft cluster of 5 servers keeps working if 2 fail, but if more fail it stops making progress rather than returning wrong results.
note: Opened raft.github.io: 'a cluster of 5 servers can continue to operate even if 2 servers fail. If more servers fail, they stop making progress (but will never return an incorrect result).' Matches.

final_text: ZooKeeper's leader election recipe: each candidate creates an EPHEMERAL|SEQUENCE znode, and the lowest sequence number is the leader. When the leader fails, its ephemeral znode disappears, and the candidate watching that znode takes over without a 'herd' of all candidates waking up.
note: Opened ZooKeeper recipes: proposals created 'with both SEQUENCE and EPHEMERAL flags'; 'The process that created the znode with the smallest appended sequence number is the leader'; 'the smallest znode will go away if the leader fails because the node is ephemeral'; watching the next znode down 'avoids the herd effect'. Matches.

final_text: AWS Application Load Balancer's 'least outstanding requests' algorithm sends each request to the target with the fewest in-progress requests; AWS says it is commonly used when requests vary in complexity or targets vary in processing capability.
note: Opened ALB target-group attributes: 'routes requests to the targets with the lowest number of in progress requests'; 'commonly used when the requests being received vary in complexity, the registered targets vary in processing capability.' AWS describes a typical use, not a recommendation; reworded.

final_text: nginx's least_conn takes server weights into account, and when several servers tie for the fewest active connections it tries them in weighted round-robin order.
note: Opened nginx upstream module, least_conn: 'passed to the server with the least number of active connections, taking into account weights of servers. If there are several such servers, they are tried in turn using a weighted round-robin balancing method.' Matches; corrects the item's 'picks at random'.

final_text: If every target in an AWS ALB target group fails its health checks, the load balancer fails open and routes to all targets regardless of health.
note: Opened ALB health checks page: 'If a target group contains only unhealthy registered targets, the load balancer routes requests to all those targets, regardless of their health status ... the load balancer fails open.' Matches.

final_text: AWS's Builders' Library distinguishes liveness, local and dependency (deep) health checks. A deep check that includes a shared dependency such as the database can fail on every server at once; load balancers then fail open, and automation that removes 'unhealthy' servers can make the outage worse.
note: Opened the AWS Builder Center copy of 'Implementing health checks' (Amazon Builders' Library article). It defines liveness, local and dependency checks; dependency checks 'can also have false positives when there are problems with the dependency itself'; 'Correlated reasons include outage of a shared dependency'; 'when all servers fail health checks at the same time, the load balancer fails open'. It does not say the fleet is taken out of service (fail-open prevents that); reworded.

final_text: Besides active health checks, nginx does passive checks: after max_fails failed attempts within fail_timeout (default 10 s) a server is marked unavailable for fail_timeout, so real request failures remove a dead backend between checks.
note: Opened nginx upstream module: max_fails is the number of unsuccessful attempts 'in the duration set by the fail_timeout parameter to consider the server unavailable for a duration also set by the fail_timeout parameter'; fail_timeout 'By default ... 10 seconds'. Matches.

final_text: Redis Pub/Sub is at-most-once: if a subscriber is disconnected or errors, the message is lost. Redis Streams persist messages and support at-least-once delivery.
note: Opened Redis Pub/Sub docs: 'Redis' Pub/Sub exhibits at-most-once message delivery semantics'; 'If the subscriber is unable to handle the message (for example, due to an error or a network disconnect) the message is forever lost.'; Streams 'support both at-most-once as well as at-least-once delivery semantics.' Matches.

final_text: Prometheus keeps data in its own local TSDB in two-hour blocks with a write-ahead log; local storage is single-node, and remote write sends samples to external clustered or durable stores.
note: Opened Prometheus storage docs (3.15): 'local on-disk time series database'; samples 'grouped into two-hour blocks'; 'write-ahead log (WAL)'; local storage 'not clustered or replicated'; external storage via 'remote read/write APIs'. Matches.

final_text: Prometheus collects metrics by pulling (scraping) targets over HTTP; pushing is supported through an intermediary Pushgateway intended for short-lived jobs.
note: Opened Prometheus overview: 'time series collection happens via a pull model over HTTP'; 'pushing time series is supported via an intermediary gateway'; 'push gateway for supporting short-lived jobs'. Matches; corrects the item's 'agents push to Prometheus'.

final_text: AWS ELB returns the IPs of its load balancer nodes via DNS; as traffic changes it scales and updates the DNS entry, using a 60-second TTL so IPs can be remapped quickly.
note: Opened 'How Elastic Load Balancing works': DNS returns 'the IP addresses of the load balancer nodes'; 'Elastic Load Balancing scales your load balancer and updates the DNS entry. The DNS entry also specifies the time-to-live (TTL) of 60 seconds.' Matches.

final_text: In Route 53 weighted routing a weight-0 record gets no traffic; if all non-zero records fail their health checks, Route 53 answers with the zero-weight records, giving active-passive failover.
note: Opened Route 53 weighted routing: 'If you want to stop sending traffic to a resource, change the weight for that record to 0'; 'If all the records that have a weight greater than 0 are unhealthy, then Route 53 considers the zero-weighted records.' Matches.

final_text: Google's Maglev runs many load-balancer machines for the same services: routers spread packets evenly across the Maglev machines with ECMP, and consistent hashing plus connection tracking keep each connection on the same backend.
note: Opened the Maglev publication page: 'Network routers distribute packets evenly to the Maglev machines via Equal Cost Multipath (ECMP)'; 'Maglev is also equipped with consistent hashing and connection tracking features'. The abstract does not literally say 'the same service IP'; reworded to what the abstract states.

final_text: nginx 'hash $key consistent' uses ketama consistent hashing, so adding or removing a server remaps only a few keys; a plain hash can remap most keys.
note: Opened nginx upstream module, hash: 'If the consistent parameter is specified, the ketama consistent hashing method will be used ... only a few keys will be remapped'; plain hash 'may result in remapping most of the keys'. Matches.

final_text: Standard Reserved Instances for Linux/UNIX can be modified to other sizes within the same instance family and generation, as long as the total instance-size footprint stays the same.
note: Opened EC2 'Modify Reserved Instances': instance size can be changed 'within the same instance family and generation', Linux/UNIX only, and 'The original and new Reserved Instance must have the same instance size footprint.' Matches (the page allows this for Convertible RIs too).

final_text: On Linux the ephemeral local port range defaults to 32768-60999, which bounds how many simultaneous connections one LB IP can open to a single backend ip:port (about 28k).
note: Opened kernel ip-sysctl docs: ip_local_port_range 'The default values are 32768 and 60999 respectively.' (28,232 ports). The per-destination bound is a direct consequence of the 4-tuple; matches.

final_text: AWS ALB uses connection multiplexing: requests from many client connections can share a single backend connection, so the number of open backend connections does not equal how busy a target is.
note: Opened 'How Elastic Load Balancing works': 'Both Classic Load Balancers and Application Load Balancers use connection multiplexing. This means that requests from multiple clients on multiple front-end connections can be routed to a given target through a single backend connection.' Matches.

final_text: EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking lets you pick a metric such as ASGAverageCPUUtilization and a target (e.g. 50%); Auto Scaling creates and manages the CloudWatch alarms that trigger scale-out and scale-in.
note: Opened EC2 Auto Scaling target tracking: 'you select a metric and a target value'; 'Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling creates and manages the CloudWatch alarms'; predefined ASGAverageCPUUtilization; 50% CPU example. Matches.

final_text: Standard ZooKeeper watches are one-time triggers sent to the client that set them, and a client sees the watch event before it sees the new data, so it must set a new watch after each event. Since ZooKeeper 3.6 a client can instead set persistent (optionally recursive) watches that stay registered.
note: Opened ZooKeeper Programmer's Guide: 'Standard watches are one time triggers'; sent to the client that set them; 'A client will see a watch event for a znode it is watching before seeing the new data'. But since 3.6.0 'Clients can also set permanent, recursive watches on a znode that are not removed when triggered', so 'must re-register after each event' applies only to standard watches; reworded.

final_text: For every scrape target Prometheus records 'up' = 1 if the target was reachable and 0 if the scrape failed.
note: Opened Prometheus 'Jobs and instances': up is '1 if the instance is healthy, i.e. reachable, or 0 if the scrape failed.' Matches.

final_text: gRPC's client-side weighted round robin computes per-backend weights from backend-reported utilization and QPS, delivered per call or out-of-band, so load-aware routing is possible without a query per request.
note: Opened gRPC proposal A58: 'The weight of a backend is calculated using utilization, QPS (queries per second), and EPS (errors per second)'; 'Either per-call or periodic out-of-band (OOB) load reporting is active at a time'. Matches.

final_text: CoreDNS's loadbalance plugin acts as a round-robin DNS load balancer by randomizing the order of A, AAAA and MX records in each answer.
note: Opened CoreDNS loadbalance plugin: 'The loadbalance will act as a round-robin DNS load balancer by randomizing the order of A, AAAA, and MX records in the answer.' Matches.

final_text: AWS ALB can authenticate users through an OIDC identity provider or Amazon Cognito before forwarding, passing signed user claims to targets in the x-amzn-oidc-data header.
note: Opened ALB 'Authenticate users': supports an OIDC-compliant IdP and Amazon Cognito user pools; 'x-amzn-oidc-data: The user claims, in JSON web tokens (JWT) format', signed by the load balancer (ES256). Matches; useful nuance (authentication can be offloaded, authorization stays in the service).

final_text: In one command: SET q <token> NX EX 300 sets the key only if it is absent and attaches the expiry atomically. Use this rather than SETNX followed by EXPIRE: if the client dies between those two calls, the lock never expires.
note: Opened Redis SET docs: NX 'Only set the key if it does not already exist', EX seconds; pattern 'SET resource-name anystring NX EX max-lock-time'; 'SET command options can replace SETNX, SETEX'. Opened SETNX docs: syntax 'SETNX key value' (no expiry argument). The crash-between-calls risk is reasoning, not quoted, and is correct.

final_text: Redis docs say the lock value 'must be unique across all clients and all lock requests', for example 20 random bytes or a timestamp concatenated with a client ID. A bare host name is not enough when several processes or retries on one host can contend.
note: Opened Redis distributed-locks page: value 'must be unique across all clients and all lock requests'; 'We assume it's 20 bytes from /dev/urandom'; 'a UNIX timestamp with microsecond precision, concatenating the timestamp with a client ID' (page adds 'not as safe'). The quote is verbatim.

final_text: Since Redis 8.4 the safe release needs no Lua: DELEX key IFEQ my_random_value deletes the key only if its value matches. On older versions use the get-compare-del Lua script with EVAL.
note: Opened Redis distributed-locks page: 'DELEX key IFEQ my_random_value'; 'The DELEX command was introduced in Redis 8.4. On previous Redis versions, this could be accomplished with the following Lua script'. Matches (checked 2026-10-13).

final_text: The owner check prevents deleting someone else's lock, but it does not stop consumer 1 from continuing its work after its lock expired, while consumer 2 also works. The standard fix is a fencing token: a number that increases with each lock grant and is sent with every write, so the storage service rejects writes from an older holder.
note: Opened Kleppmann: fencing token is 'a number that increases (e.g. incremented by the lock service) every time a client acquires the lock'; the storage server 'rejects the request with token 33'. Opened Redis distributed-locks page: 'You should implement fencing tokens.' Matches.

final_text: Redlock's acquire rule has two conditions: the client locked a majority (at least 3 of 5) AND the total time spent acquiring is less than the lock validity time. The usable validity is then the TTL minus the time spent acquiring.
note: Opened Redis distributed-locks page step 3: 'If and only if the client was able to acquire the lock in the majority of the instances (at least 3), and the total time elapsed to acquire the lock is less than lock validity time'; step 4: validity is 'the initial validity time minus the time elapsed'. Matches.

final_text: A client that fails to get the majority should try to unlock all instances, 'even the instances it believed it was not able to lock'. A SET may have succeeded even though its reply was lost. It should then retry after a random delay so that competing clients do not keep colliding.
note: Opened Redis distributed-locks page step 5: 'it will try to unlock all the instances (even the instances it believed it was not able to lock)'; Retry on Failure: 'try again after a random delay in order to try to desynchronize multiple clients'. The lost-reply explanation is implied by 'can be performed whether or not the client believes it was able to successfully lock'. Quote is verbatim.

final_text: Redis's documented fix for this edge case is 'delayed restarts': keep a crashed instance unavailable for a bit longer than the max lock TTL, so every lock it held has expired before it rejoins. The alternative is AOF persistence with fsync=always, at a performance cost.
note: Opened Redis distributed-locks page: 'make an instance, after a crash, unavailable for at least a bit more than the max TTL'; 'delayed restarts'; 'we need to enable fsync=always ... This will affect performance'. Matches.

final_text: Redis's own Redlock page adds two consistency caveats. First, implement fencing tokens; don't assume a lock is retained as long as the process that acquired it is alive. Second, Redis does not use a monotonic clock for TTL expiry, so a wall-clock jump can let two processes hold the lock.
note: Opened Redis distributed-locks page, 'Disclaimer about consistency': 'You should implement fencing tokens.'; 'don't assume that a lock is retained as long as the process that had acquired it is alive'; 'Redis is not using monotonic clock for TTL expiration mechanism ... a wall-clock shift may result in a lock being acquired by more than one process.' Paraphrase is faithful.

final_text: Kleppmann's rule of thumb: if a lock exists only for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work), a single Redis instance is enough. If it protects correctness, use a consensus system such as ZooKeeper with fencing tokens rather than Redlock.
note: Opened Kleppmann: for efficiency 'You are better off just using a single Redis instance'; for correctness 'use a proper consensus system such as ZooKeeper', with fencing. Matches.

final_text: Long jobs don't need a long TTL. The holder can extend the lease while it is still working (Redis: a Lua script that resets the TTL only if the key still holds its value). The DynamoDB Lock Client does the same with periodic heartbeats against a lease (example: 3 s heartbeat, 10 s lease).
note: Opened Redis distributed-locks page, 'Extending the lock': 'sending a Lua script to all the instances that extends the TTL of the key if the key exists and its value is still the random value'. Opened AWS DynamoDB Lock Client blog: sample uses .withLeaseDuration(10L) and .withHeartbeatPeriod(3L) seconds; owner heartbeats to renew. Matches.

final_text: MySQL has named locks built in: GET_LOCK('q7', timeout) returns 1 if acquired. The lock is released by RELEASE_LOCK() or 'implicitly when your session terminates (either normally or abnormally)', so a crashed holder does not leave a perpetual lock. It is local to a single mysqld.
note: Opened MySQL 8.4 locking functions: GET_LOCK 'Returns 1 if the lock was obtained successfully'; released by RELEASE_LOCK() 'or implicitly when your session terminates (either normally or abnormally)'; 'GET_LOCK() establishes a lock only on a single mysqld'. Quote is verbatim.

final_text: ZooKeeper's lock recipe: each client creates an ephemeral sequential znode under the lock path. The lowest sequence number holds the lock, and every other client watches only the node just before it, so a release wakes exactly one waiter, with no polling or timeouts. Ephemeral nodes are deleted when the holder's session ends.
note: Opened ZooKeeper recipes (Locks): lowest sequence number holds the lock; exists() watch on 'the next lowest sequence number'; 'There is no polling or timeouts'; avoids the herd effect. Opened Programmer's Guide: ephemeral znodes exist 'as long as the session that created the znode is active'. Matches.

final_text: SQS standard queues are at-least-once: a copy of a message can come back if a server was unavailable during delete. A message also becomes visible again if processing outlasts the visibility timeout. AWS asks consumers to be idempotent; RabbitMQ likewise says consumers 'must be prepared to handle redeliveries'.
note: Opened SQS at-least-once page: 'you might get that message copy again'; 'Design your applications to be idempotent'. Opened ReceiveMessage API: if not deleted before the visibility timeout 'it becomes visible again and can be retrieved by other consumers'. Opened RabbitMQ 4.3 confirms: 'consumers must be prepared to handle redeliveries'. Matches; quotes verbatim.

final_text: In a MongoDB transaction, a conflicting lock request does not wait for commit: by default it waits up to 5 ms, then the transaction aborts and the client retries. A non-transactional write to a document locked by a transaction does wait until the transaction ends.
note: Opened MongoDB production considerations (9.0 current): 'By default, transactions wait up to 5 milliseconds to acquire locks ... If the transaction cannot acquire its required locks within the 5 milliseconds, the transaction aborts.'; 'when a write outside the transaction tries to modify the same document, the write waits until the transaction ends.' Matches.

final_text: TCP alone may not detect a dead peer quickly. If the client's host crashes or is cut off, the server's socket stays open until the application times out or TCP keepalive fires. On Linux, keepalive is off unless SO_KEEPALIVE is set and starts only after 7200 s idle by default.
note: Opened tcp(7): 'Keep-alives are sent only when the SO_KEEPALIVE socket option is enabled'; tcp_keepalive_time 'The default value is 7200 seconds (2 hours).' The host-crash case is correct reasoning. Matches.

final_text: dpkg's lock is not 'does the file exist?'. Frontends take an fcntl(2) advisory record lock on <admindir>/lock-frontend and then <admindir>/lock (/var/lib/dpkg on Debian/Ubuntu). The kernel drops such locks automatically when the process terminates, so a crash never leaves a stale lock.
note: Opened dpkg frontend-api.txt: acquire 'the frontend lock at <admindir>/lock-frontend' 'and then acquire the dpkg database lock at <admindir>/lock'; 'These locks must be file record locks (i.e. fcntl(2) advisory locking)'. Opened fcntl_locking(2): 'record locks are automatically released when the process terminates.' The /var/lib/dpkg default admindir is not on the spec page but is the standard Debian path. Matches.

final_text: For scale: a round trip inside one datacenter is about 0.5 ms (Jeff Dean's figures, ~2012), and AWS describes latency between Availability Zones in a region as single-digit milliseconds. A 3-10 ms budget per service hop therefore includes much more than wire time: serialization, TLS, queueing and the handler itself.
note: Opened jboner gist: 'Round trip within same datacenter 500,000 ns 500 us', table labelled '(~2012)'. Opened AWS fault-isolation whitepaper: AZs are 'close enough to use synchronous replication with single-digit millisecond latency'. The last sentence ('Most of the 3-10 ms per service hop is therefore serialization, TLS, queueing and handler time') is the checker's inference and no source says it; softened.
